Steller's sea eagle (Haliaeetus pelagicus) is one of the largest raptors in the world and exhibits a relatively slow life history, typical of many long-lived apex predators. Field data from the Russian Far East indicate that females lay two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], reflecting the substantial energetic investment required to rear such large offspring. Newly hatched chicks are remarkably small given the parents' immense size; the initial wet weight of a hatchling is approximately 165 grams [Ww0 = approximately 165 grams]. This modest neonatal mass is supported by a rich yolk reserve that sustains the chick through the first critical days of development. The incubation period, during which the egg is maintained at an average temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], lasts for approximately 41.5 days [ab = approximately 41.5 days], a duration that is consistent among large Haliaeetus eagles. This relatively protracted incubation reflects the heat transfer constraints of a large egg with a thick calcareous shell. At the moment of hatching, the chick itself weighs approximately 110 grams [Wwb = approximately 110 grams], somewhat less than the initial egg mass owing to metabolic consumption of yolk reserves and water loss during incubation.

Once hatched under the thermal conditions typical of the nesting season, which often sees ambient nest temperatures rise to around 40 °C [T = 40 °C] during the warmest part of the day, the nestling cycle proceeds through several key milestones. The most dramatic early transformation is the rapid gain in body mass; chicks that weighed just 165 grams at hatching are provisioned intensively by both parents. By the time of fledging, the young eagle has attained a substantial fraction of adult mass. The fledgling period, defined as the age at first sustained flight, occurs at 70 days after hatching [tx = 70 days after hatching] under these warm conditions at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This developmental pace is relatively fast for a bird of this ultimate body size, driven by a diet rich in salmon and carrion that provides abundant protein. Even after fledging, the immature bird remains dependent on parental food deliveries for several additional weeks, honing its flight and hunting skills before achieving true independence.

As the young Steller's sea eagle continues to mature, its growth trajectory and timing of key life-history events are tightly linked to the abundant seasonal food supply of the subarctic coastal environment. Sexual maturity, defined by the attainment of adult plumage and functional gonads, is a delayed process in this species. Under the typical ambient thermal regime of the breeding grounds, where active metabolic rates are maintained at roughly 40 °C [T = 40 °C], males reach puberty at 210 days after hatching [tp = 210 days after hatching]. This relatively early gonadal maturation does not immediately translate into breeding activity, as young eagles must first establish territories and acquire the physical prowess required to compete with older, more experienced conspecifics. The sub-adult period is characterized by a slow increase in body mass and the gradual replacement of juvenile flight feathers with the distinctive white tail and shoulder feathers of the adult. Full adult body size is not achieved until several years of age, reflecting the extreme upper end of the size range for accipitriform raptors.

The physical dimensions of adult Steller's sea eagles are truly impressive and exhibit pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a common feature among large piscivorous raptors where females are larger. The ultimate wet weight for adult females, representing the asymptotic maximum body mass attained by fully grown individuals in prime condition, is approximately 7885 grams [Wwi = approximately 7885 grams]. Males, by contrast, are considerably lighter, with an ultimate wet weight of about 5500 grams [Wwi = about 5500 grams]. This half-kilogram difference in mass is reflected in their foraging ecology, with the smaller and more agile males often taking a broader range of prey, while the larger females tend to dominate the richest feeding sites along salmon streams. The maintenance of this massive body size imposes high daily energetic costs, requiring a constant influx of food throughout the non-breeding season. Consequently, the age at first successful breeding in these eagles is significantly delayed compared to smaller-bodied raptors.

Given the substantial energy demands and the time required to secure a high-quality territory on the Kamchatka coastline, first-time breeding is deferred for many years. Longitudinal studies of marked individuals suggest that the age at first reproduction, defined as the time since birth when a bird successfully lays its first brood, occurs at approximately 5 years after hatching [tR = approximately 5 years after hatching] under the typical thermal conditions of their active period (40 °C [T = 40 °C]). This late onset of reproduction is a classic component of a slow life-history strategy, balancing high adult survival against low fecundity. Indeed, the maximum lifespan of this species is remarkably long; well-documented records from both the wild and captive populations indicate that individuals can live for 25 years [am = 25 years] under natural conditions at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This exceptional longevity, combined with a low reproductive rate of just a single clutch per year, makes the population highly sensitive to increases in adult mortality from anthropogenic sources such as lead poisoning and habitat degradation.
